title: Mottle and the Moonlight Melon
markdown:
Deep in the winding valleys of Hazelhowe, where the wind sang silly tunes through rocky nooks and ferns curled like sleepy green dragons, lived a little goblin named Mottle. He had a cozy home, a dear goblin mother, and a nose that twitched when he was excited. What he wanted most was to seem clever and perfectly organised. This was a pickle. His shoelaces tied themselves into grumpy knots, and his grand plans often tumbled like a wobbly tower of acorns.

One breezy afternoon his mother, apron smelling of warm bread and happy thoughts, said, “Mottle, my dear, would you fetch a basket of the sweet-smelling moonpetal herbs from the edge of the Whispering Woods? I need them for my special evening stew. They’ll make it extra fragrant.”

He puffed his chest. A grand chance. He spotted an old slightly lopsided wizard hat belonging to Great-Uncle Fizzwick, a goblin of notable charm who once made tea that tasted suspiciously like fizzy lemonade. Midnight blue. Silver stars that seemed to wink even in sunshine. With a wiggle that nearly sent him tumbling, Mottle plopped it on. A tad too big. It tickled his nose and gave him a look of perpetual surprise, as if he had just remembered the kettle. He felt it lent him an air of wizardry. He imagined riddles solved with a flick of pointy ears.

“Fear not, Mother,” he declared, a little muffled by the brim. “Your most organised son shall return with the finest moonpetal herbs Hazelhowe has ever known. Perhaps even a sprinkle of enchanted dew for extra sparkle.” He tried to sound brave. A small flutter started in his tummy, a trapped butterfly that had not asked to come.

He grabbed an empty basket, wicker smooth and familiar, and set off with a determined stride. The woods felt known. Mossy rocks like velvet. Little brooks singing bubbly songs. He hummed a goblin tune, hat bobbing. He was so busy picturing his mother’s proud smile, and maybe honey cakes, that he did not quite notice when the path stretched and twisted like a playful ribbon. Sunlight dappled through leaves in shifting patterns. Familiar trees looked like friendly giants waving hello, which is not the same as knowing where you are.

“Now, where did Mother say those herbs were?” he mumbled, adjusting the hat. It tilted, revealing a patch of sky the colour of bruised plums. Evening was drawing near. Near a cluster of plump red-capped fungi a tiny flickering light: Glimmer, a glow-worm Mottle knew from less-organised days spent watching fireflies. The light pulsed gently, a shy heartbeat.

“Hello, Glimmer. I am on a very important errand for my mother. A quest, you might say.”

Glimmer’s light brightened. “Evening, Mottle,” whispered the glow-worm, dry-leaf rustle. “The woods have a way of stretching when the sun dips low. They like to play hide-and-seek with paths. The moonpetal herbs are usually by the gnarled oak, the one with the face like a grumpy old man. But the shadows are growing long, and the night air is sweet with something else tonight. Something different.”

Mottle blinked. The shadows were long, inky fingers across the floor, making the world mysterious and grand. A faint sweet scent, not the familiar lemony tang of moonpetals, drifted on the air. Summer breezes and forgotten dreams. His toes gave a little wiggle, then a tremor rippled up his legs. The sort of flutter Mother got before a big storm. He pushed it down and blamed the wind. He was Mottle, clever, organised, wearing a wizard hat. Practically a magician.

He marched on. The hat slipped further. Trees thinned. He found himself in a clearing bathed in unusual soft moonlight, though the moon itself only peeked from behind a fluffy cloud, as if the whole clearing had been dipped in moonlight paint. In the centre sat a melon. What a melon. Enormous. Bigger than Mottle. Bigger than his mother’s prize stew pot. It shimmered with a faint pearly luminescence, as if it held captured starlight in its rind. The scent was heavenly. His tummy rumbled with anticipation.

Beside it, shadow long and wobbly like a friendly giant stretching after a nap, stood a mountain of an ogre. Hands like clumps of rich dark soil, big enough to scoop a whole basket of berries. Voice like cupboards full of forgotten teacups. Grumbles, the ogre gardener, known throughout Hazelhowe for prize-winning moonlit vegetables said to outshine any firefly. Mottle froze. Feet glued to dewy grass. The hat slipped completely over his eyes and plunged him into darkness.

“Well, well,” rumbled Grumbles, peering down with eyes surprisingly kind, like warm embers. “What’s this little sprout lost in my garden? Did you get yourself tangled in the beanstalks?”

Mottle, forgetting moonpetal herbs and wizardly impressing, pushed the hat up with one elbow. The ogre’s face looked less like a scowl and more like a sleepy badger who had just woken from a pleasant dream. Not terrifying. Just big. And very protective of his magnificent melon. He stroked its shimmering skin with surprising tenderness.

Mottle took a deep breath of sweet melon air. This was not the clever magic he had planned with a borrowed hat. “Good evening, Mr Grumbles, sir,” he squeaked, voice trembling like a leaf. “I seem to have wandered. I was looking for moonpetal herbs for my mother’s stew, and I seem to have found your magnificent melon instead. It’s truly spectacular.” He patted his pockets. Nothing. No herbs. No clever spells. Not even a shiny pebble. The basket remained stubbornly empty.

Grumbles grunted, a chest-deep rumble, but his eyes twinkled like the stars on Mottle’s hat. “Moonpetal herbs, eh? Those are over yonder, near the babbling brook. Easy to miss when you’re distracted by prize-winning produce. This here is my prize moonlight melon. Grown with a touch of moonlight and a whole lot of patience. And a bit of talking to it every morning, mind you. They do enjoy a good chat.” He stroked the pearly skin again, a fond smile.

Mottle felt a prickly disappointment. He had forgotten his errand. He was far from organised. He had come to be clever and had only got lost. Then, looking at the melon, he noticed a small straggly weed, quite out of place, tugging rather impudently at the base of the glorious fruit, as if it meant to steal all the moonlight nourishment.

“That weed,” he said, pointing with a tentative finger, voice gaining a little confidence. “It looks a bit out of sorts. It might be taking nourishment from your lovely melon, sir. Perhaps it’s a bit greedy.”

Grumbles squinted and bent low. “Hmph. Never noticed that little chap trying to get ideas above his station.” Enormous hands, surprisingly delicate, pulled the weed free, roots and all. A tiny sigh of relief seemed to come from the ground.

“Oh, thank you,” Mottle said, a rush of something warmer than pride, sunshine spreading. A small thing. It felt important.

Grumbles chuckled, dry leaves in a gentle breeze. “You know, for a lost sprout, you’ve got a good eye. Noticing the little things is important. And that hat. Rather festive. Makes you look as if you’re about to pull a rabbit out of somewhere unexpected.” He winked. “Tell you what. Since you pointed out that pesky weed, and you seem like a decent sort who respects a good garden, I’ll share a slice of my moonlight melon with you. It’s quite scrumptious, though it does taste best shared.”

He produced a knife as long as Mottle’s arm, gleaming in the moonlight, and cut a generous wedge that held its own quiet shine. The scent was a symphony of sweetness. Mottle took a bite. It tasted like the sweetest dream he had ever had, cool and refreshing, honey and the soft glow of night woven into the flavour. Better than the honey cakes he had imagined.

Carrying the slice carefully, the fruit almost as big as his head, he thanked Grumbles profusely. With a much clearer idea of the way home, guided by the friendly ogre’s directions, he set off. The hat still slipped over his eyes now and then. It did not matter quite so much. He had performed no grand magic. He had not been organised in the way he had planned. He had found a delicious adventure and a wonderfully kind ogre.

He arrived home not with moonpetal herbs but with a story that shimmered brighter than any enchanted dew and a slice of moonlight melon that shone like a captured star. His mother saw his beaming face and the fruit that still held the night in it, and she set two bowls, and they ate stew that was fragrant enough without the herbs, because the table had a story on it. She did not mention the hat slipping. She cut the melon and smiled as if that were the cleverest thing a son could bring.
